title: F1 in Texas: The American race that fans love to attend
gist: Ars's visit to the US Grand Prix at COTA looks at why the permanent Austin track is the American race that real fans attend, and talks to Audi F1 racing director Allan McNish about the team's first year, bumpy surface, automated hybrid energy management and a 2030-oriented roadmap. Antonelli won easily and is close to the title.

themes.theme: COTA as the fan-oriented US F1 venue

insights.claim: COTA, once in danger of falling off the calendar due to lack of interest, is now one of the most popular tracks on the F1 calendar and, of the US's three races, the one the real fans mostly attend.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: F1's US growth is not limited to the glitzy street-circuit races.
insights.quote: it’s the one the real fans mostly attend

insights.claim: Unlike Miami or Las Vegas, COTA is a permanent track with run-off areas rather than concrete walls, and it was designed by motorcycle racer Kevin Schwanz, with Herman Tilke's company only doing buildings and infrastructure, contrary to popular belief.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Track design pedigree affects the racing product versus the temporary circuits.

insights.claim: COTA has diversified into a theme park, concert venue and race track, with hospitality structures including a cable-car-linked one with two swimming pools, and rollercoasters on its fringes, since the first USGP in 2012.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Venues are monetizing beyond race weekends through entertainment diversification.
insights.locator: It’s changed a lot since I attended

insights.claim: The track layout is unchanged in 14 years, but the surface gets bumpier each year due to the earthworks that create the elevation changes and the extremes of central Texas weather.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Track wear is a growing operational concern for teams and drivers.
insights.locator: The basic track layout hasn’t changed

insights.claim: 2026 is Audi's first year as an official F1 constructor after completing its purchase of Sauber in 2024; with no prior experience in the sport it has hardly embarrassed itself.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Audi's entry is on a credible but slow path, consistent with a long-horizon investment.
insights.quote: 2026 is Audi’s first year as an official F1 constructor

insights.claim: McNish says Audi is consistently fighting in and around Q3, and its best result of the year came in Singapore, with cars in the points in sprint, qualifying and race for the first time, after losing points on the last lap in the previous two races.
insights.speaker: Allan McNish
insights.quote: We’re consistently fighting in and around Q3

insights.claim: Audi brought aerodynamic upgrades to COTA, a second part after one at Baku, intended to add performance in the first sector, and the work is aimed at next year rather than this season.
insights.speaker: Allan McNish
insights.so_what: Development resources are being shifted toward next season.

insights.claim: McNish says Audi's roadmap looks toward 2030, not just 2027, and predicts the top four teams next year will remain the top four because it does not change overnight.
insights.speaker: Allan McNish
insights.so_what: Audi is unlikely to challenge the front in the near term, so investors should expect a long payback.
insights.quote: I think what you will find next year is that the top four teams will be the top four teams

insights.claim: The Audi car is good in medium- and high-speed corners but weaker out of slow corners and in straight-line speed, partly because of the choice of a larger turbocharger, taken to ensure a robust, reliable power unit in the first season.
insights.speaker: Allan McNish
insights.so_what: A reliability-first trade-off cost performance this year.
insights.locator: Right now, the Audi is good

insights.claim: Sauber used a Ferrari power unit until last year, so Ferrari holds the data on it rather than Audi, and every circuit is new to Audi.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Audi starts without historic data, which slows its learning curve.
insights.quote: Ferrari has all that data, not Audi

insights.claim: At COTA, Audi's rookie Gabi took a 20-place grid penalty for power-unit component changes and finished P13, while Hulkenberg lost places at the start when the anti-stall kicked in, then recovered to P11, just outside the points.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Power unit penalties and reliability are still costing Audi points.
insights.locator: It was a less successful day

insights.claim: The new power units were unreliable, which was to be expected given breakdowns in 2014, the first year of the last engine rules, and this year's hybrid systems have come under fire for being complicated and unpredictable; earlier reports of AI/ML use were overstated.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Complex new regulations produce reliability costs in early years, and the AI narrative around F1 is overhyped.
insights.quote: earlier reports this season about the use of AI/ML were overstated

insights.claim: McNish says energy deployment profiles are predetermined from simulator work but must adapt on the day, and Audi hones its profiles each race, with prediction differing from race reality.
insights.speaker: Allan McNish
insights.so_what: Real-time adaptation remains human-driven, not AI-driven.

insights.claim: The 2014 energy-per-lap regulation was very manual and impossible for drivers, so power unit control was quickly automated to free their mental bandwidth; McNish says the more you can take away from the driver the better.
insights.speaker: Allan McNish
insights.so_what: Regulations that overload humans get automated, which shifts the competitive differentiation to engineers.
insights.quote: the more you can take away from the driver, the better it is

insights.claim: Racing is adaptive as fuel load falls, tires degrade, grip rises and the track cools, and the driver must still maximize the car, so there is lots of communication.
insights.speaker: Allan McNish
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop is retained because conditions change during the race.

insights.claim: Antonelli took pole and won comfortably, extending his championship lead, and George Russell needs 23 points more than him in Mexico City to remain in contention, with Hamilton needing 24, so Antonelli will almost certainly clinch next time out, becoming F1's youngest champion.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The title is effectively decided, which limits late-season intrigue.
insights.quote: we’ll almost certainly see Antonelli seal the deal next time out
insights.locator: The race itself was not one
